lf-derinkuyu.t: Derinkuyu: who dug a city 85 metres under Turkey, and when?
lf-derinkuyu.d:
In 1963, in central Turkey, a man knocking through his basement wall found a room he never knew was there. Below it lay a city cut into soft volcanic rock, about 85 metres deep, with stables, wells, a church and doors made of stone wheels. It is one of hundreds of underground shelters in Cappadocia.

Who dug them, and when? We weigh what can be dated (crosses, churches, Byzantine pottery, written accounts of raids and refugees) against the boldest claim, Ice Age shelters older than the Flood, and show why carving erases its own history. Verdicts: Byzantine refuges, Established; Ice Age shelters, Awaiting evidence.

lf-sky-fell.t: Did a Comet Bring Back the Ice Age? The Younger Dryas, Weighed
lf-sky-fell.d:
About 12,900 years ago, as the last Ice Age was letting go, the north plunged back into the cold for some 1,200 years: the Younger Dryas. Since 2007 a team of scientists has argued that a comet, or its fragments, set it off and left a thin layer of clues on four continents. Most specialists blame meltwater that stalled the Atlantic.

We weigh both camps at their strongest: the black mat and its microspherules and nanodiamonds, the Greenland platinum spike, the melted glass of Abu Hureyra, the Carolina Bays, the failed replications and the fight over dates, the meltwater routes, the newest papers and retractions, and why it all matters for the first farmers. The verdict on the comet: Awaiting evidence.

lf-troy.t: Was the Trojan War Real? The Hill of Nine Cities
lf-troy.d:
A low hill in northwest Turkey holds nine cities, one on top of another, and high in the stack, a layer of fire from around 1180 BCE. Was this Homer's Troy, and was there really a Trojan War?

We follow the dig from Frank Calvert's trial trenches and Heinrich Schliemann's great trench to the walls of Troy VI and Manfred Korfmann's lower town; read what Hittite tablets say about a western kingdom called Wilusa; sort what Homer seems to remember from the Bronze Age from what he added; and set the fire against the collapse of a whole world. Verdict: Strong evidence for a real, rich city destroyed around the time Greek tradition places the war. The war as Homer tells it remains an Open question.

lf-sea-peoples.t: The Sea Peoples: Who Really Ended the Bronze Age?
lf-sea-peoples.d:
Around 1177 BCE, Ramesses III had a sea battle carved on his temple at Medinet Habu: ships with a bird's head at each end, warriors in feathered crowns and horned helmets. In the same decades, palaces from Greece to Syria burned or were abandoned, and the last king of Ugarit wrote that enemy ships had burned his cities.

Did the Sea Peoples bring down the Bronze Age world? We weigh six suspects one by one: raiders and migrants (the Medinet Habu texts, the last letters of Ugarit, ancient DNA from Philistine Ashkelon), drought (lake cores and the tree rings of Gordion), hunger, earthquakes, broken trade and revolt, and the idea of a perfect storm. Verdict: Mixed record.

lf-alexandria.t: What Really Happened to the Library of Alexandria?
lf-alexandria.d:
Everyone knows the Library of Alexandria burned in one great fire. The ancient writers tell a stranger, slower story: a king who drove the scholars out, a Roman general's fire in the harbour, a war that wrecked the palace quarter, a temple torn down, and a tale of a caliph's bonfire first written down nearly six centuries late.

We follow the library from its founding under the first Ptolemies, through the books seized from ships, the borrowed Athenian originals and Callimachus' great catalogue, then weigh every ending against the evidence, and close on what was lost and what survived. Verdict on 'one great fire': Ruled out.

lf-mkultra.t: MKUltra: The CIA Destroyed the Files. Seven Boxes Survived
lf-mkultra.d:
In 1973, the CIA destroyed the files of MKUltra, its secret programme of drug and behaviour experiments. Four years later, seven forgotten boxes of its financial records turned up anyway: receipts for work at universities, hospitals and prisons, much of it paid through front foundations.

We follow what those surviving files show: the Cold War fear of brainwashing, Allen Dulles's approval in 1953 and Sidney Gottlieb's programme, LSD given to people who did not know in safe houses in New York and San Francisco, the death of Frank Olson and the questions his family raised, the 1977 Senate hearing, and the patients of the Allan Memorial Institute in Montreal. Then we weigh it: drug experiments on unwitting people, Established; mind control that works, Awaiting evidence; and the destroyed files leave gaps nobody can see into.

lf-first-americans.t: Ice Age Footprints: When Did People Reach the Americas?
lf-first-americans.d:
Small footprints in the mud of a vanished lake in New Mexico, many of them made by teenagers and children in the depths of the last Ice Age. For much of the twentieth century, the textbooks said people reached the Americas only about 13,000 years ago. How did that wall of dates fall, and what still stands?

We follow the Clovis points, the long fight over Monte Verde in Chile and its new challenge in 2026, the caves of Oregon and a riverbank in Idaho, the White Sands footprints and the argument over their dates, the two roads past the ice, and what ancient genomes say about the ancestors of Native Americans. Verdict on people in the Americas by about 21,000 years ago: Strong evidence.

lf-arthur.t: Was King Arthur Real? What the Earliest Sources Say
lf-arthur.d:
In 1191, the monks of Glastonbury Abbey said they had dug up a lead cross that read: here lies buried the renowned King Arthur, in the isle of Avalon. Was there ever a real King Arthur?

We read the sources in the order they were written: Gildas, born in the year of the battle of Badon, who never names Arthur; the line "he was no Arthur" in the Welsh poem Y Gododdin; the History of the Britons of about 829, with its twelve battles; the Welsh Annals, with Badon and Camlann; then Geoffrey of Monmouth, who made Arthur a king, and the French poet who named Camelot. We weigh the Glastonbury grave, follow the digs at Cadbury Castle and Tintagel, meet the candidates from Riothamus to Artorius, and grade each piece of the legend. Verdict: Open question. A real war-leader may lie behind the name, but no source from his own lifetime names him.

lf-vinland.t: Vikings in America: How a Solar Storm Gave Us the Year
lf-vinland.d:
A thousand years ago, someone cut wood with a metal blade at the northern tip of Newfoundland, and a storm on the Sun, frozen in the tree rings, gives us the year: 1021. Did the Norse really reach America nearly five centuries before Columbus? And where was the land of grapes their sagas called Vinland?

We read the two Vinland sagas and where they disagree; follow Helge Ingstad and Anne Stine Ingstad to the grassy bumps of L'Anse aux Meadows and the eight buildings beneath them; date the wood with the cosmic-ray signal of 993; follow three butternuts south to New Brunswick; ask, with care, who the people the sagas met really were; and test the claims that did not hold: the Vinland Map, the Kensington Runestone and Point Rosee. Verdict: Established for the Norse at L'Anse aux Meadows around 1021. The Vinland Map and the Kensington Runestone: Ruled out. Where Vinland was, and how long the Norse stayed: Open question.

lf-knossos.t: Was the Minotaur's Labyrinth Real? The Palace of Knossos
lf-knossos.d:
A palace wall on Crete painted with a young acrobat flying over a charging bull. A Greek myth of King Minos, a maze and a monster, half man and half bull. And a clay tablet from the same palace that sends honey to the Mistress of the Labyrinth. Was the Labyrinth a real place?

Verdict: Plausible. The myth plausibly remembers a real palace, a bull cult and a sea power. Whether the palace itself was the Labyrinth is an Open question. A living Minotaur is Ruled out.

lf-stargate.t: The US Paid Psychic Spies for 23 Years. Did It Work?
lf-stargate.d:
In the summer of 1974 a former police commissioner at the Stanford Research Institute in California drew a giant crane he had never seen, at a secret Soviet site about 10,000 km away. CIA analysts judged the crane accurate. From 1972 to 1995, the United States government paid for remote viewing: describing distant targets by the mind alone.

We follow what the declassified files show: the Cold War fear of Soviet psychic research, the CIA's first money for Russell Targ and Harold Puthoff's work with Ingo Swann and Pat Price, the Army unit at Fort Meade and its code names, how a session worked and why judging a hit is so hard (the clues David Marks and Richard Kammann found in the transcripts, and the matches that felt uncanny but were wrong), and the 1995 review for the CIA in which Jessica Utts and Ray Hyman disagreed about the lab statistics while the operational record was found to be of no use. Verdict on remote viewing as reliable intelligence: Ruled out. The programme itself: Established. A psychic effect in the lab: Awaiting evidence.

Verdict: Ruled out for an ice-free Antarctica on the map. Strong evidence that the map keeps part of a lost chart by Columbus.
